name: Surveyor 3
physicalFate: The lander remains on the Moon in Oceanus Procellarum. Apollo 12 astronauts visited it in 1969 and returned selected parts to Earth.
missionObjective: Surveyor 3 tested a soft landing and studied the lunar surface before crewed Apollo landings.
howItWorked: A television camera, soil-mechanics scoop, and simple instruments observed the ground and tested how a lander could settle on lunar soil.

hardwareDiagram.title: Surveyor 3 lander, documented hardware view
hardwareDiagram.description: A NASA photograph provides the hardware view. The component labels identify only hardware documented for Surveyor 3; select one to learn what it did.

components.label: Television camera
components.explanation: Surveyor 3's camera returned images of the lunar surface and landing site.
components.importance: It let mission teams see the terrain and assess the landing environment.

components.label: Soil-mechanics scoop
components.explanation: The scoop disturbed and sampled lunar soil near the lander.
components.importance: Its work helped characterize the strength and texture of lunar soil.

components.label: Surface instruments
components.explanation: Surveyor 3 carried simple instruments that observed the surface and supported its landing investigation.
components.importance: Together, these measurements tested what a lander would encounter on the Moon.

discoveries: It returned more than 6,000 television images of the lunar surface.
Its scoop helped characterize the strength and texture of lunar soil.
Apollo 12 found that some exposed materials had changed during their time on the Moon.
whyItMatters: Surveyor 3 was both a robotic geologist and a rehearsal for humans working safely on the Moon.

timeline.description: It lands in Oceanus Procellarum after two engine shutdowns and restarts.

name: Apollo 12 lunar hardware
physicalFate: The Apollo 12 lunar module descent stage, ALSEP experiments, cameras, and other equipment remain at the landing site in Oceanus Procellarum. Individual instruments have different operational histories.
missionObjective: Apollo 12 made a precision lunar landing, inspected Surveyor 3, and deployed a long-lived package of lunar science experiments.
howItWorked: The ALSEP package used separate instruments to measure moonquakes, the lunar environment, and the Moon's interior and surface properties.
discoveries: ALSEP experiments returned data about lunar seismic activity and the environment.
The crew collected samples near a known robotic landing site.
The landing demonstrated precision navigation for future lunar fieldwork.
whyItMatters: Apollo 12 connected a robot's measurements with human geology and left a scientific station on another world.

name: Spirit
physicalFate: Spirit remains embedded in Martian soil at the site NASA named Troy, near Gusev Crater. NASA ended its recovery effort after the rover stopped communicating.
missionObjective: Spirit investigated rocks and soil in Gusev Crater for evidence of past water activity.
howItWorked: Solar panels powered a six-wheeled mobile laboratory with panoramic cameras, a robotic arm, and instruments that examined rock chemistry.
discoveries: It found evidence that ancient water altered rocks in Gusev Crater.
It climbed Husband Hill and explored layered volcanic terrain.
It operated for years beyond its planned 90-sol mission.
whyItMatters: Spirit showed that a small, carefully designed machine could turn a crater into a readable geological record.

name: Opportunity
physicalFate: Opportunity remains at Perseverance Valley in Meridiani Planum. A planet-encircling dust storm covered its solar arrays and ended communications.
missionObjective: Opportunity studied rocks and soils in Meridiani Planum for geological evidence of ancient water.
howItWorked: Solar arrays powered six wheels, cameras, a robotic arm, and spectrometers that identified minerals in Martian rocks and soil.
discoveries: It found hematite concretions nicknamed blueberries.
It identified rocks shaped by ancient acidic water.
It drove farther on another world than any previous NASA rover.
whyItMatters: Opportunity made the history of Martian water visible in ordinary-looking rocks.

name: Curiosity
physicalFate: Curiosity is operating on Mars in Gale Crater, exploring Mount Sharp. Its radioisotope power system is designed for long-duration surface science.
missionObjective: Curiosity investigates whether Mars ever had environments able to support microbial life.
howItWorked: A nuclear-powered rover drills rocks, carries samples into an onboard laboratory, and uses cameras and weather instruments to study its surroundings.
discoveries: It found ancient freshwater lake environments in Gale Crater.
It detected organic molecules in Martian rocks.
It measured changing methane and radiation conditions at the surface.
whyItMatters: Curiosity tests habitability with a mobile chemistry lab instead of only looking at rocks from a distance.

name: Perseverance
physicalFate: Perseverance is operating in Jezero Crater. It has cached rock samples for a possible future return to Earth and carried the Ingenuity helicopter to Mars.
missionObjective: Perseverance searches for signs of ancient microbial life, characterizes geology, and collects carefully selected samples.
howItWorked: Its cameras and instruments inspect rocks, a drill seals samples in tubes, and a small helicopter tests powered flight in the thin Martian atmosphere.
discoveries: It explored an ancient river-delta environment in Jezero Crater.
It demonstrated powered flight on another planet with Ingenuity.
It has collected and sealed geologically diverse rock samples.
whyItMatters: Perseverance is building a geological library that future missions could bring to Earth for laboratory study.

name: Voyager 1
physicalFate: Voyager 1 is traveling through interstellar space. Its radioisotope generators provide declining power for a limited set of instruments and communications.
missionObjective: Voyager 1 studied Jupiter and Saturn before continuing outward to investigate the space between stars.
howItWorked: A dish antenna communicates with Earth while radioisotope generators convert plutonium decay heat into electricity.
discoveries: It revealed active volcanoes on Io.
It found a thin ring around Jupiter.
It crossed the heliopause into interstellar space.
whyItMatters: Voyager 1 transformed a short outer-planet flyby mission into a decades-long experiment at the edge of the Sun's influence.

name: Voyager 2
physicalFate: Voyager 2 is traveling through interstellar space after its encounters with all four giant planets. Its power and instrument set are gradually being reduced.
missionObjective: Voyager 2 was designed to visit the outer planets and continue studying the heliosphere beyond them.
howItWorked: Gravity assists bent its path from planet to planet, saving fuel while its instruments measured fields, particles, atmospheres, and rings.
discoveries: It is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune.
It discovered active geysers on Neptune's moon Triton.
It crossed the heliopause in 2018.
whyItMatters: Voyager 2 completed the only close-up survey of all four giant planets and keeps extending that map outward.

name: New Horizons
physicalFate: New Horizons continues through the Kuiper Belt after its Pluto and Arrokoth encounters. NASA periodically places the spacecraft in hibernation to conserve power.
missionObjective: New Horizons was built for the first close reconnaissance of Pluto and its moons, then extended to study Kuiper Belt objects.
howItWorked: A compact radioisotope-powered spacecraft used cameras, spectrometers, and a dust detector during fast flybys.
discoveries: It revealed Pluto's nitrogen-ice heart and surprisingly varied geology.
It made the first close encounter with a Kuiper Belt object, Arrokoth.
It continues measuring the distant outer Solar System.
whyItMatters: New Horizons showed that even a small, fast spacecraft can rewrite the map of a world glimpsed only as a point of light.

name: Pioneer 10
physicalFate: Pioneer 10 continues on a heliocentric escape trajectory beyond the outer planets, but its radioisotope power declined until NASA could no longer hear it. Its exact current condition is not observable from Earth.
missionObjective: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to travel through the asteroid belt and make a close encounter with Jupiter.
howItWorked: Its instruments measured particles, magnetic fields, radiation, and the environment around Jupiter while a large dish antenna sent faint signals back to Earth.
discoveries: It showed that a spacecraft could safely cross the asteroid belt.
It made the first close-up study of Jupiter and measured its intense radiation environment.
Its observations helped plan later missions to the outer planets.
whyItMatters: Pioneer 10 was a pathfinder: it tested whether a machine could survive the route to the outer Solar System before more ambitious missions followed.

name: Pioneer 11
physicalFate: Pioneer 11 continues outward on a heliocentric trajectory. It is silent after its final communication in 1995, so its present engineering condition cannot be directly checked.
missionObjective: Pioneer 11 followed Pioneer 10 with close studies of Jupiter and Saturn, including the first visit to Saturn by a spacecraft.
howItWorked: A spin-stabilized probe used instruments for fields, particles, radiation, and imaging while its radio system returned measurements across enormous distances.
discoveries: It made the first close encounter with Saturn and helped reveal the planet’s polar regions and rings.
It found a new ring and a previously unknown moon at Saturn.
It provided a valuable radiation and dust survey for later missions.
whyItMatters: Pioneer 11 extended the pathfinder idea from Jupiter to Saturn and made the outer Solar System a reachable place for spacecraft.
